title: The walls of Jericho (Joshua 6)
hook: six days of silent circling, then shofar blasts and a shout

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger with a sword, and Joshua barefoot. Your line was holy ground again. Did you stop for a breath somewhere ordinary? Today, the city itself. Day seven hundred two.

For six days, the only sound around Jericho is the shofar. Armed men walk in front. Then seven priests, blowing seven rams' horns as they go. Then the ark. Then everyone else. Row after row of feet, and not one human voice. The instruction was clear: no shouting, no talking, not a word from your mouth until the day you're told. Once around the walls, back to the camp for the night. The next morning, again. Behind its walls, Jericho is shut tight, facing an army that doesn't attack.
screen: `SIX DAYS OF SHOFAR.` → `NOT ONE HUMAN VOICE.` → `AN ARMY THAT DOESN'T ATTACK.`

segments.voice: On the seventh day they rise at dawn and go around, not once, but seven times. On the seventh circuit the priests blow, and Joshua finally gives the word: shout, for the Lord has given you the city. The people raise a great shout, and "the wall fell down flat." Notice what the story leaves out. No battering ram. No ladders. No tunnel under the wall. The city is taken by a strange discipline: patience, silence, repetition, and then one sound at the right moment. The instruction had said it plainly: no word from your mouth until the day I bid you shout, "then shall ye shout." Now listen to the shout itself. The Hebrew for that great shout is teruah. It's also the name of a shofar call. When the Torah describes Rosh Hashanah, it calls it a day of teruah, a day of blowing the horn. So the same word holds a people's cry and the ram's horn of the new year. Some readers hear in Jericho a picture of the Days of Awe: circle, wait, keep quiet, and then let out the sound you've been holding. And there's a hard part, and the book doesn't hide it. The city is put under the ban, and its people are killed, and readers wrestle with that command. Inside the destruction, one promise holds. Before the city burns, the two spies go into Rahab's house and bring out her and her whole family, as they swore they would. The spies kept their word.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `NO RAM, NO LADDER: SILENCE.` · `TERUAH: A SHOUT, A SHOFAR CALL.` · then, large: `THE WALL FELL DOWN FLAT.` · then: `RAHAB'S FAMILY BROUGHT OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk around something in silence. A table, a chair, a bed, the room you're in. Walk slowly, once around, without a word. Then again. Notice your feet, the edges, what you usually walk past without seeing. If you can't walk, let your eyes go slowly around the edges of the room instead, once, then again. Keep the silence the whole way. When you stop, stand or sit still and let the quiet settle before anything else is said. The bell holds the time.
The walls of Jericho. Six days of silent circling behind the shofar, seven times on the seventh, and then the shout. Today's word.
Your line: circle, then shout. Today, be patient and quiet with one thing that won't move yet, and when the moment comes, say what needs saying. Day seven hundred two.

howItsDone: On Rosh Hashanah the shofar is sounded in synagogue in a set series of calls, among them teruah, a run of quick short blasts.

what a scholar hears: teruah. the people's great shout and the shofar call of Rosh Hashanah, the day of teruah, share one word.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording of 'the wall fell down flat' (6:20) and 'then shall ye shout' (6:10).
The counts (seven priests, seven shofars, six days, seven circuits on the seventh day) are taken directly from Joshua 6:3–15.
Teruah in Joshua 6:20 and in Numbers 29:1 (yom teruah); the link to the Days of Awe is framed as 'some readers hear'. Confirm.
The ban (herem) and killing in 6:21 is named briefly and honestly; a Keeper may want different wording.
howItsDone: description of the teruah call as short broken blasts; confirm.
